title: Frank Costello
wiki_lead:
Frank Costello (Italian: [koˈstɛllo]; born Francesco Castiglia [franˈtʃesko kaˈstiʎʎa]; January 26, 1891 – February 18, 1973) was an Italian-American mafioso and boss of the Luciano crime family (later known as the Genovese crime family) in New York City from 1938 to 1957. Known as the “Prime Minister of the Underworld”, Costello was noted for his political connections and for a leadership style that emphasized diplomacy and business dealings. His televised testimony at the 1951 Kefauver Committee hearings caught nationwide attention and brought public awareness to the extent of organized crime in the United States.
Born in Calabria, Italy, he moved with his family to the United States as a child. As a youth he joined gangs in New York City. Working with Charlie “Lucky” Luciano, Costello was involved in bootlegging operations during Prohibition. In 1929 they joined the National Crime Syndicate. After Luciano was imprisoned in 1936, he continued to run the family from prison through acting boss Vito Genovese. In 1937, Genovese fled to Naples to avoid a murder indictment in New York. Following this, Luciano appointed Costello, who had risen to the rank of consigliere, as the new acting boss. After the United States Supreme Court refused to review Luciano’s case in October 1938, Costello became boss of the Luciano crime family, although Luciano continued to wield considerable power and influence within the American Mafia.
In the 1950s, Costello was convicted of tax evasion and served time in prison. In 1957, he survived an assassination attempt in which he was shot in the head outside his Manhattan apartment building by Vincent Gigante, acting on the orders of Genovese. However, the bullet only grazed his head. Costello subsequently retired, with Genovese succeeding him as boss of the family, which became known as the Genovese crime family. He remained largely out of the spotlight for the remainder of his life until his death from a heart attack in 1973 at the age of 82.

Early life
Costello was born Francesco Castiglia on January 26, 1891, in Lauropoli, a frazione of the town of Cassano allo Ionio in the province of Cosenza in the Calabria region, Italy. In 1895, he boarded a ship to the United States with his mother and his brother Edward to join their father, who had moved to New York City's East Harlem several years earlier and opened a small neighborhood Italian grocery store.
While Costello was still a boy, his brother introduced him to gang activities. At 13, he had become a member of a local gang and started using the name Frankie. Costello committed petty crimes and went to jail for assault and robbery in 1908, 1912, and 1917.
On September 22, 1914, Costello married Loretta "Bobbie" Geigerman, a Jewish woman, whose parents had immigrated from the German Empire. That same year, Costello served ten months in jail for carrying a concealed weapon.

grok_lead: Frank Costello (born Francesco Castiglia; January 26, 1891 â February 18, 1973) was an Italian-born American mobster who became a leading figure in New York City's organized crime, serving as acting boss of the Luciano crime family and earning the nickname "Prime Minister of the Underworld" for his influence and mediation skills within the Mafia. Immigrating to the United States from Italy's Calabria region at age four, Costello engaged in street crime and burglaries in Manhattan's East Harlem before rising through the ranks during Prohibition, partnering with Lucky Luciano and Meyer Lansky in bootlegging operations that laid the foundation for the national crime syndicate. He controlled extensive gambling enterprises, including slot machines and bookmaking across New York, Louisiana, Florida, and Cuba, amassing significant wealth while forging political alliances that shielded his activities. Costello's career included testifying before the Kefauver Committee in the early 1950s, where his refusal to invoke the Fifth Amendment drew scrutiny, leading to convictions for tax evasion and contempt that he partially served before prevailing on appeal. In 1957, he survived an assassination attempt orchestrated by rival Vito Genovese, shot in the head by Vincent Gigante but recovering to retire from direct control of the family, ceding power while maintaining advisory influence until his death from a heart attack.
